children: Short interest in five U.S. airlines has been in a broad uptrend this year as their stocks have moved opposite to oil since the Iran war began in February, according to S3 Partners Director of Research Leon Gross.
Average short interest in the airline group rose from 8% to 13% of float, S3 said. JetBlue Airways
went from 20% to 29%, the largest increase in percentage points. Short interest in American Airlines
S3 said that makes short sellers effectively long oil and means they do not expect the war to end soon. Investors in the oil ETF
, by contrast, hold a large net short position.
Fuel is the airlines' largest cost risk because it is volatile, Gross said. A large drop in oil would send the stocks higher.

S3's chart showed the airline average trading within about 20% of its start-of-year level. It swung from positive to negative when the war began and fell about 30% from its pre-war high. JetBlue fell about 36% from its pre-war high to its March low. USO reached roughly 235% of its January level in September, by eye.

Long interest in the group stayed in a 29% to 35% range for most of the year, rose in September, and has since eased. JetBlue's rose from 25% to 36%, first as its stock fell with higher oil and then further in September with the sector.

JetBlue's losses widened in 2026, primarily because of soaring jet fuel prices driven by the war, along with higher wages and severe weather disruptions, S3 said. It is also struggling with heavy debt service costs and strategic pressure as it expands in Florida after Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May 2026.
, and Alaska have made money in each whole calendar year for five years, S3 said. American has recently been close to breakeven.
